final_proof:
There is a small but essential point about the wording. A discrete family in the usual sense is a topological notion, whereas the hypotheses call X only a set and do not give it a topology. The relation-theoretic conclusion that the hypotheses do imply—and that proves the intended topological assertion whenever the V_k are diagonal neighborhoods—is the following:

For every n > 0 and every p in X, the set V_{n+2}[p] meets at most one member of A_n.

Here R[x] := {z in X : (x,z) in R}. We use the convention that (x,z) is in R composed with S if there is t with (x,t) in S and (t,z) in R; thus U_{n+1} = V_{n+1} composed with U_n.

Fix n > 0 and p in X. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that V_{n+2}[p] meets A_n(x) and A_n(y) for two distinct indices x and y. Choose

  a in V_{n+2}[p] intersect A_n(x), and b in V_{n+2}[p] intersect A_n(y).

Because the ordering is a well-order, it is in particular total. After interchanging x,a with y,b if necessary, assume x is strictly earlier than y. Since a and b both belong to V_{n+2}[p], we have (p,a) and (p,b) in V_{n+2}. Symmetry gives (a,p) in V_{n+2}; hence

  (a,b) in V_{n+2} composed with V_{n+2},

and the square condition gives (a,b) in V_{n+1}. Also a in A_n(x) implies a in U_n[x], so (x,a) is in U_n. Consequently

  (x,b) in V_{n+1} composed with U_n = V_{n+1} composed with V_n composed with ... composed with V_1 = U_{n+1}.

Thus b is in U_{n+1}[x]. But x is strictly earlier than y, while the definition

  A_n(y) = U_n[y] minus the union of U_{n+1}[z] over all z strictly earlier than y

excludes every point of U_{n+1}[x] from A_n(y). This contradicts b in A_n(y). Therefore V_{n+2}[p] meets at most one member of A_n, as claimed.

If X has a topology for which V_k[p] is a neighborhood of p for every k and p (in particular, in the intended setting where each V_k is a neighborhood of the diagonal in X times X), then V_{n+2}[p] is a neighborhood of p meeting at most one member of A_n. Since p was arbitrary, A_n is a discrete family. To justify the parenthetical assertion: if V_k contains an open set G with the diagonal contained in G, then openness of G at (p,p) gives open neighborhoods O and N of p with O times N contained in G; since p is in O, N is contained in V_k[p].

If no such topological neighborhood hypothesis is intended, the literal topological claim is false (indeed, no topology was specified). For a concrete counterexample, give X = {0,1} the indiscrete topology, well-order it by 0 < 1, and put V_k = Delta_X for every k. All stated relation hypotheses hold, U_n = Delta_X, and A_n(0) = {0}, A_n(1) = {1}. The family {{0},{1}} is not discrete in the indiscrete topology, because the only neighborhood of either point is X, which meets both members. Thus the corrected theorem is the relation-ball assertion above, or equivalently the stated conclusion with the added assumption that every V_k[p] is a neighborhood of p.
